title: The Story of the Vizier Who Was Punished
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a king whose son loved to hunt. The king often let him ride out, but he had ordered his grand vizier to go along every time and never let the prince out of his sight. One day the huntsman flushed a stag, and the prince, assuming the vizier was right behind him, went after it and rode so hard that he ended up alone. He pulled up, and since the stag was gone, he turned back to find the vizier, who had not been attentive enough to keep up. But the prince had lost his way. While he was searching for the road, he noticed a beautiful woman at the roadside, weeping bitterly. He reined in his horse and asked who she was, what she was doing in such a place, and whether she needed help. “I am the daughter of an Indian king,” she replied. “I was riding in the countryside when I fell asleep and slipped from my horse. It bolted, and I have no idea where it has gone.”

The young prince felt sorry for her and offered her a seat behind him on his horse, and she accepted. When they came to a ruined building, the woman climbed down and went inside. The prince got down as well and followed her. To his great shock, he heard her call to someone within, “Rejoice, my children! I have brought you a nice plump young man.” Other voices answered, “Where is he, mamma? Let us eat him right now, we are so hungry!”

The prince saw at once the peril he was in. He understood now that the woman who called herself an Indian king’s daughter was an ogress, one of those creatures that live in lonely places and use a thousand tricks to catch travelers and devour them. Terrified, he threw himself onto his horse. Just then the false princess came out, and seeing that her prey had escaped her, she said, “Don’t be afraid. What do you want?”
“I am lost,” he said, “and I am trying to find the road.”
“Keep going straight,” said the ogress, “and you will come to it.”

The prince could scarcely believe what he had heard, and he galloped away as fast as he could. He found the road and reached his father’s house safe and unharmed, and there he told the king of the danger he had faced because of the grand vizier’s negligence. The king flew into a rage and had the vizier strangled on the spot.

“Sire,” the vizier went on, speaking to the Greek king, “let us come back to the physician Douban. If you are not careful, you will regret trusting him. Who can say that this remedy that cured you will not turn out, in time, to do you harm?”
The Greek king was a weak man by nature. He did not see the vizier’s evil purpose, and he lacked the strength to stand by his first decision.
“Very well, vizier,” he said, “you are right. Perhaps he did come to take my life. He could do it with nothing more than the scent of one of his drugs. I must think what to do.”
“Sire,” said the vizier, “the surest way to protect your life is to summon him now, and have his head cut off the moment he arrives.”
“Yes,” the king answered, “I truly think that is the best course.”
He told one of his ministers to bring the physician, and the physician came at once.
“I have sent for you,” said the king, “so that I can be rid of you by taking your life.”
The physician was utterly astonished to hear that he was to die.
“Your majesty, what crimes have I committed?”
“I have learned,” the king answered, “that you are a spy and mean to kill me. But I will strike first, and kill you. Strike!” he ordered an executioner standing nearby. “Free me from this assassin.”
At this cruel command the physician fell to his knees. “Spare my life,” he cried, “and yours will be spared.”

Here the fisherman broke off to say to the genie, “You see, what happened between the Greek king and the physician has just happened between the two of us. The Greek king,” he continued, “showed him no mercy, and the executioner blindfolded him.”
Everyone in the room begged for the physician’s life, but it was no use.

Bound and kneeling, the physician said to the king, “At least give me time to put my affairs in order and leave my books to people who will make good use of them. There is one I would like to give to your majesty. It is very precious, and should be kept safely in your treasury. It holds many curious things, and the chief of them is this: after my head has been cut off, if your majesty will turn to the sixth leaf and read the third line of the left-hand page, my head will answer any question you care to put to it.”

The king, eager to see so wonderful a thing, postponed the execution until the next day and sent the physician home under heavy guard. There the physician settled his affairs, and the next day a great crowd filled the hall to watch him die and to see what would happen afterward. The physician came to the foot of the throne carrying a large book. He also brought a basin, over which he spread the book’s cover, and offering it to the king, he said, “Sire, take this book. When my head has been cut off, have it set in the basin on the cover of this book. As soon as it is there, the blood will stop flowing. Then open the book, and my head will answer your questions. But sire, I beg you for mercy, because I am innocent.”
“Your pleading is wasted, and even if it were only to hear your head speak after you are dead, you will die.”
With that he took the book from the physician’s hands and told the executioner to do his work.

The head was cut off so skillfully that it dropped right into the basin, and the blood stopped flowing at once. Then, to the king’s great amazement, the eyes opened, and the head said, “Your majesty, open the book.” The king did, and finding that the first leaf was stuck to the second, he put his finger in his mouth to wet it so that it would turn more easily. He did the same for each page until he reached the sixth, and seeing no writing on it, he said, “Physician, there is nothing written here.”

“Turn a few more pages,” the head replied. The king kept turning, wetting his finger in his mouth each time, until the poison that coated every page took hold. His sight failed, and he collapsed at the foot of his throne.
When the physician’s head saw that the poison had done its work and that the king had only a few minutes left, it cried, “Tyrant, see how cruelty and injustice are punished.”
No sooner had it spoken than the king died, and the head lost what little life it had left.
So ends the story of the Greek king, and now we go back to the fisherman and the genie.
“If the Greek king had spared the physician,” said the fisherman, “he would not have died like that. The same goes for you. Now I am going to throw you into the sea.”
“My friend,” said the genie, “don’t do anything so cruel. Do not treat me the way Imma treated Ateca.”
“What did Imma do to Ateca?” the fisherman asked.
“Do you think I can tell you that while I am shut up in here?” replied the genie. “Let me out, and I will make you rich.”
The hope of never being poor again made the fisherman yield.
“If you give me your promise that you will do this, I will take off the lid. I do not think you would dare to go back on your word.”

The genie gave his promise, and the fisherman lifted the lid. The genie rose out in a cloud of smoke, and once he had taken his true shape again, the first thing he did was kick the jar into the sea. This frightened the fisherman, but the genie laughed and said, “Don’t be afraid. I only did that to scare you, and to show you that I mean to keep my word. Take your nets and follow me.”

He set off walking in front, and the fisherman followed him with some misgivings. They passed the town, climbed up a mountain, and then went down into a great plain, where a large lake lay between four hills.
When they reached the lake, the genie said to the fisherman, “Cast your nets and catch some fish.”

The fisherman did as he was told, expecting a good catch, since he could see plenty of fish. How amazed he was to find that there were four entirely different kinds, some white, some red, some blue and some yellow. He caught four, one of each color. He had never seen any like them, so he admired them greatly, and he was delighted to think how much money they would bring.

“Take these fish to the Sultan, and he will pay you more for them than you have ever had in your life. You may come and fish in this lake every day, but take care to cast your nets only once a day, or something bad will happen to you. If you follow my advice closely, you will be glad of it.”
As he said this, he stamped his foot on the ground, and it opened. He vanished into it, and it closed again at once.
The fisherman made up his mind to follow the genie’s orders exactly. He cast his nets only once, then headed into town to sell the fish at the palace.

When the Sultan saw the fish, he was greatly amazed. He looked at them one by one, and when he had admired them long enough, he said to his first vizier, “Take these fish and give them to the skilled cook that the Emperor of the Greeks sent me. I imagine they taste as good as they look.”
The vizier carried them to the cook himself, saying, “Here are four fish that were brought to the Sultan. He wants you to cook them.”

Then he returned to the Sultan, who told him to give the fisherman four hundred gold pieces. The fisherman had never held so much money at one time and could hardly believe his luck. He immediately saw to his family’s needs and put the money to good use.

But now we must go back to the kitchen, where we will find great confusion. When the cook had cleaned the fish, she put them in a pan with oil to fry. When she judged them done on one side, she turned them over. But hardly had she done so when the kitchen wall opened and a beautiful young woman stepped out. She wore Egyptian dress of flowered satin, with earrings, a necklace of white pearls, and gold bracelets set with rubies, and in her hand she held a wand of myrtle.

She walked up to the pan while the cook, astonished, stood frozen at the sight of her. She tapped one of the fish with her wand and said, “Fish, fish, are you doing your duty?” The fish gave no answer. She asked again, and this time they all lifted their heads together and replied, very clearly, “Yes, yes. If you count, we count. If you pay what you owe, so do we. If you run, we win, and we are content.”
When they had spoken, the young woman overturned the pan and went back into the opening in the wall, which closed at once and looked exactly as it had before.
Once the cook got over her fright, she picked the fallen fish out of the ashes. They were burned black as coal, no use to serve the Sultan, and she started to weep.
“Oh no! What will I tell the Sultan? He will be so angry with me, and I know he won’t believe me!”

While she was crying, the grand vizier came in and asked whether the fish were ready. She told him everything that had happened, and he was very surprised. He sent for the fisherman at once, and when the man arrived he said, “Fisherman, bring me four more fish like the ones you brought before, because something has happened to them and they can’t be served to the Sultan.”
The fisherman did not mention what the genie had told him. He excused himself from bringing them that day because of the long distance, and promised to bring them the next day.
That night he went to the lake and cast his nets, and when he pulled them in he found four fish like the others, each a different color.
He went straight back and delivered them to the grand vizier, as he had promised.

The vizier then took them to the kitchen and shut himself in with the cook, who began to cook them just as she had cooked the other four the day before. When she was about to turn them over, the wall opened and the young woman appeared. She spoke the same words to the fish, received the same answer, then overturned the pan and disappeared.
The grand vizier was filled with amazement. “I will tell the Sultan everything that has happened,” he said, and he did.

The Sultan was astounded and wanted to witness this marvel himself. He sent for the fisherman and asked him to get four more fish. The fisherman asked for three days, which were granted, and then he cast his nets in the lake and once more caught four fish of different colors. The Sultan was delighted to have them and again gave him four hundred gold pieces.
As soon as the Sultan had the fish, he had them taken to his own room, together with everything needed to cook them.

Then he shut himself in with the grand vizier, who began to prepare and cook them. When they were done on one side, he turned them over. Then the wall of the room opened, but instead of the young woman, a black slave came out. He was enormously tall and carried a large green staff, with which he touched the fish, saying in a terrible voice, “Fish, fish, are you doing your duty?” At these words the fish raised their heads and replied, “Yes, yes. If you count, we count. If you pay what you owe, so do we. If you run, we win, and we are content.”
The black slave overturned the pan in the middle of the room, and the fish were reduced to cinders. Then, with a proud stride, he went back into the wall, and it closed behind him.
“After seeing that,” said the Sultan, “I cannot rest. These fish point to some mystery that I must get to the bottom of.”
He sent for the fisherman. “Fisherman,” he said, “the fish you brought us have disturbed me. Where did you get them?”
“Sire,” he answered, “I got them from a lake in the middle of four hills, beyond those mountains over there.”
“Do you know this lake?” the Sultan asked the grand vizier.
“No,” said the vizier. “I have hunted around that mountain many times, but I have never heard of it.”
The fisherman said it was only three hours away, so the Sultan ordered his entire court to mount and ride there, with the fisherman leading the way.

They climbed the mountain, and on the far side they saw the lake just as the fisherman had described it. The water was so clear that they could see the four kinds of fish swimming in it. They watched them for a while, and then the Sultan ordered a camp to be set up at the water’s edge.

That night the Sultan summoned his vizier. “I’ve made up my mind to get to the bottom of this mystery,” he said. “I’m going out alone. You stay here in my tent, and when my ministers come tomorrow, tell them I’m unwell and can’t see them. Keep doing that every day until I come back.”

The grand vizier did his best to talk the Sultan out of it, but it was no use. The Sultan took off his robe of state and buckled on his sword, and once he saw that the camp was quiet, he slipped away alone.

He climbed one of the hills and crossed the wide plain beyond it, and at sunrise he saw a huge building far ahead of him. As he drew closer, he could see it was a magnificent palace of polished black marble, plated with steel as smooth as a mirror.
The gate was standing half open. He knocked, and when nobody came, he walked in. He crossed a grand courtyard and still met no one, though he called out several times.

He passed through great halls with silk carpets, with couches and sofas upholstered in tapestry from Mecca, and with hangings of the finest Indian fabrics, woven with gold and silver. Then he came into a splendid chamber with a fountain held up by golden lions. The water that streamed from the lions’ mouths turned into diamonds and pearls, and the jets leapt up until they nearly touched the exquisitely painted dome. Magnificent gardens, small lakes and woods surrounded the palace on three sides. Birds sang in the trees, which were covered with nets so that the birds could never fly away.
Still the Sultan saw nobody, until he heard a mournful cry and a voice saying, “If only I could die! I am too wretched to want to go on living!”

The Sultan looked around to find who was lamenting his fate like this. At last he saw a handsome young man in rich clothes, seated on a throne set a little above the floor. His face was full of sorrow.
The Sultan went up to him and bowed. The young man lowered his head deeply but did not stand.
“Sire,” he said to the Sultan, “I can’t get up and show you the respect I know your rank deserves.”
“Sir,” the Sultan answered, “I’m sure you have good reason. I heard your cry of anguish, and I have come to offer you my help. Whose palace is this, and why is it so empty?”
Instead of replying, the young man raised his robe and showed the Sultan that from the waist down he was a block of black marble.
The Sultan was appalled and asked the young man to tell him what had happened.
“I will gladly tell you my sad story,” said the young man.
